answers.text: Tell it: always return exactly three lines - delivery date, item and quantity, and any change from the original order - in that order, using the same labels each time. If a change isn't mentioned in the email, write 'no change' rather than leaving it blank.

Ask it to list every claim on its own line with date, amount, category and submitter, then total the amount column at the end. If two lines look the same, keep both but mark them as a possible duplicate instead of merging them.

The error is in the dates - the call was on the 14th, and 'three days out' should be the 17th, not the 19th as the email states. I'd check the call notes or the calendar to confirm the actual agreed date before it goes to the client.
The 15% delivery rise checks out fine. The on-time rate doesn't - 3 late out of 62 is about 95%, not the 97% the report gives.

Output 2, since it shows the €612,000 and €25,100 behind the 4.1%. Output 1 could still be correct, but there's no way to check it without rerunning the numbers yourself. Even with Output 2, I'd want to confirm those two source figures are right first.

Reply 2 - it has the order reference and the credit reference, so both can be checked. Reply 1's 'entirely our error' isn't something you can verify as it stands. I wouldn't rule it out completely, just confirm the dispatch date against our records before sending it.

The pricing and volume discounts are sensitive, so I wouldn't paste those in directly. The confidentiality clause naming both companies makes the whole thing worth handling carefully. The delivery schedule on its own seems fine to paste as is.
Before the weekly report goes out, I cross-check the main totals against the source system rather than just reading it over.

Step 4, sending the confirmation automatically, is the one that most needs a check since it can't be undone. Step 1 matters too, because a bad read of the order email would carry through everything after it.
